Get to know me

A designer in the making, with ideas to share.

I am a BSIT graduate of Datamex College of Saint Adeline, specializing in Web Development with a focus on UI/UX Design. I love designing apps, websites, posters, and logos, and I enjoy exploring layouts, colors, and typography that make a design feel clear and welcoming.

My strengths are creativity, curiosity, and a willingness to keep learning. I teach myself design tools like Figma and Canva, and I am learning HTML/CSS. My IT background in troubleshooting, networking, and Excel data analysis helps me understand how designs work for real users and real systems. I am honest about my level: I am still a beginner in these skills, and I am building them one project at a time.

My goal is to start my career as a Junior UI Designer who creates clean, intuitive, and user-friendly digital experiences. I value clarity, honesty, and design that puts people first. Outside of design, I enjoy learning new tools and turning ideas into something people can use.

Data project

Social media engagement analysis.

I analyzed 50 social media posts across Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok to find out which platforms and content types get the most engagement, then wrote evidence-based recommendations.

Key patterns

  • Platform efficiency: Facebook had the highest average engagement rate (9.04%), while TikTok had the largest total reach.
  • Content performance: Video had the highest engagement rate (9.15%), while Text had the highest average reach per post (5,827.75).
  • Top performers: 4 of the top 5 posts were on Facebook, and 3 of those were videos, led by P9014 at 13.99%.
RankPostPlatformTypeReachEngagementRate
1P9014FacebookVideo7,1901,00613.99%
2P9042FacebookVideo3,99350912.75%
3P9000InstagramText2,74735012.74%
4P9035FacebookImage9,5601,21612.72%
5P9043FacebookVideo4,97162912.65%

My recommendations

  1. Focus video content on Facebook. It consistently drives the highest engagement rate.
  2. Add calls-to-action on TikTok. Interactive questions or prompts can turn its large reach into more engagement.
  3. Use text posts for wide reach. Use them on Facebook and Instagram for key announcements.

How I did it

  • Tools: Excel (formulas, pivot table, charts).
  • Steps: calculated Total Engagement (likes + comments + shares) and Engagement Rate (engagement / reach), ranked the posts, summarized with mean, median, minimum and maximum, then compared platforms and content types with a pivot table.
  • Limitations: only 50 posts. Video duration was recorded for just 3 videos, so the very weak correlation (0.03) with engagement is not reliable.

Problem-solving

How I fix things.

Troubleshooting cases with the problem, causes, diagnosis, solution, and lesson learned.

Case 1: Connected to Wi-Fi but no internet

Problem: The computer shows it is connected to Wi-Fi, but websites do not open.

Possible causes: Router or modem problem, wrong IP settings, DNS problem, or a driver problem.

Diagnostic procedure: (1) Checked if other devices could use the internet. (2) Restarted the router and modem. (3) Ran ipconfig to check the IP address. (4) Ran ping 8.8.8.8 to test the connection, then ping google.com to test DNS.

Solution: Restarted the router, then ran ipconfig /flushdns and reconnected to the network.

Lesson learned: Test one cause at a time, starting from the simplest, and check whether the problem is on the device or on the network.

Case 2: Slow computer

Problem: The computer takes a long time to open programs and sometimes freezes.

Possible causes: Too many programs running, too many startup apps, low storage space, low memory, or malware.

Diagnostic procedure: (1) Opened Task Manager with Ctrl + Shift + Esc and sorted the processes by CPU, Memory, and Disk to see what used the most. (2) Checked the free storage space. (3) Checked the Startup apps list.

Solution: Closed the programs that were not needed, disabled unnecessary startup apps, freed up storage space, and restarted the computer.

Lesson learned: Find the cause of the slowness before reinstalling or replacing anything.

Case 3: No sound from the computer

Problem: No sound comes out of the speakers or headphones.

Possible causes: Muted or very low volume, wrong output device selected, loose cable or Bluetooth connection, or an audio driver problem.

Diagnostic procedure: (1) Checked the volume and mute icon on the taskbar. (2) Opened the Sound settings and checked which output device was selected. (3) Checked that the cable or Bluetooth connection was working. (4) Tested another app and another speaker or headphones.

Solution: Unmuted the sound, selected the correct output device, and reconnected the cable. Restarted the computer when needed.

Lesson learned: Check the simple settings first, because they are often the cause.

Case 4: Printer is not printing

Problem: A document is sent to print, but the printer does not print it.

Possible causes: Printer turned off or offline, no paper or ink, paper jam, a stuck print job, the wrong default printer, or a cable or Wi-Fi problem.

Diagnostic procedure: (1) Checked that the printer was on, connected, and had paper and ink. (2) Looked at the printer status for "Offline". (3) Opened the print queue to look for a stuck job. (4) Checked that the correct printer was set as default.

Solution: Cleared the stuck job from the print queue, set the printer back online, restarted the printer, and printed a test page.

Lesson learned: Check the printer status and the print queue first.

Case 5: Keyboard or mouse is not responding

Problem: The keyboard or mouse does not respond when used.

Possible causes: Loose USB connection, a faulty USB port, dead batteries for wireless devices, a driver problem, or a damaged device.

Diagnostic procedure: (1) Checked that the device was plugged in properly. (2) Tried another USB port. (3) Replaced the batteries for a wireless device. (4) Tested the device on another computer to see whether the problem was the device or the computer.

Solution: Moved the device to a working USB port or replaced the batteries, then restarted the computer.

Lesson learned: Isolate whether the problem is in the device or in the computer.

Cybersecurity case

Weak passwords: a small habit, a big risk.

A defensive case study on one of the most common security problems, and how both users and developers can prevent it.

1. What is the vulnerability?

A weak password is one that is short, common, predictable, or reused across many accounts, so it is easy for someone else to guess or crack.

2. How can it happen?

  • People choose common passwords or ones based on personal details like birthdays and names.
  • The same password is reused on many sites, so one leak exposes every account.
  • Attackers try lists of common passwords or passwords leaked from other breaches.
  • A system that allows unlimited login attempts makes guessing easier.

3. What are the risks?

  • Account takeover and stolen personal information.
  • Access to other accounts that share the same password.
  • Financial loss, identity misuse, and damaged trust.
  • For organizations, a possible data breach.

4. How can developers prevent it?

  • Require a minimum password length and check passwords against lists of common or leaked ones.
  • Store passwords only as secure hashes (for example bcrypt or Argon2), never as plain text.
  • Limit repeated failed logins with rate limiting or temporary lockouts.
  • Offer multi-factor authentication and a safe password reset process.

5. Security practices to follow

  • Use long passphrases that are easy for you to remember but hard to guess.
  • Use a different password for every account and keep them in a password manager.
  • Turn on multi-factor authentication wherever it is available.
  • Never share passwords, and change them right away if an account may have been leaked.

What did AI help me accomplish?

What did I personally verify?

What limitations did I find?

Final reflection

What I learned, in my own words.

Before BSIT

Before I entered the BSIT program, I knew almost nothing about IT. I only used computers and phones for everyday things like schoolwork and social media, and I did not know how websites, spreadsheets, or networks actually worked. IT felt like something technical that only other people understood.

What I learned

Over the course of the program, that changed. I learned the basics of troubleshooting and networking, such as checking a connection and finding the cause of a problem step by step. I learned how to use Excel to organize data, calculate results, and turn them into charts. I am also trying to learn HTML and CSS, but I am still at the very beginning and have not mastered them yet. On my own, out of curiosity, I started exploring design tools like Figma and Canva. Nobody taught me or told me to do this. It was my own choice, and it is how I discovered that I enjoy design. The most important thing I learned is that IT is not about knowing everything. It is about finding the cause of a problem, testing it, and fixing it patiently. In August 2026, I also attended two webinars, one on UI and UX for cybersecurity and IoT and another on mastering mobile development with GitHub. They showed me how design, security, and development connect.

The project that taught me the most

The project that taught me the most is this portfolio website. It was the first time I put together a complete website from start to finish. I used AI tools to help me, but I checked and corrected each part myself. Through it I am starting to understand how a web page is structured, with a head for hidden information and a body for everything visitors see, and how CSS controls color, spacing, and fonts. I also learned to present my work with evidence, because every skill I claim has to be backed by something I can show. My Social Media Engagement Analysis in Excel taught me a different lesson: numbers are only useful when I explain what they mean, such as why Facebook had the highest engagement rate.

My biggest technical difficulty

The technical difficulty that challenged me most was the layout and code of the website. My first version did not display correctly because of small mistakes in my code. A tag was missing its opening symbol, an empty tag stood where the body should have been, and my style rules were placed below the content instead of inside the head. My profile photo also did not appear at first, which taught me that file names and locations must be exact. I fixed these problems by reading my code line by line, comparing it with a correct version, and changing one thing at a time. These problems taught me patience and attention to detail, because one missing character can stop a whole page from working.

How my skills have changed

My skills have changed from almost none to being able to analyze a dataset in Excel, troubleshoot common computer problems, and put together a simple web page with AI assistance, which I then checked and corrected myself. I am still a beginner in Figma, Canva, troubleshooting, networking, and data analysis, and I am only starting to learn HTML and CSS. I want to be honest about that. I still need to improve my Figma prototyping, keep practicing HTML and CSS until I can build pages without help, and create more complete projects.

The IT professional I want to become

I want to become a UI designer who combines creativity with an understanding of how real systems work, so that every design is both attractive and easy to use. My IT background helps me communicate with developers and understand technical limits.

Why I am ready

I am ready to begin my career in IT because I can show evidence of what I have learned: a portfolio website, a data analysis project, troubleshooting and security case studies, an AI usage log, and certificates. I know I am at the beginning of my journey, but I am ready to take a junior role, learn from experienced people, and keep growing.

1. Tell me about yourself.

I'm Sofia Bianca Junto, a BSIT graduate of Datamex College of Saint Adeline. I focus on Web Development with an interest in UI/UX design. I started with almost no IT background, and since then I've learned troubleshooting and networking basics, Excel data analysis, and I taught myself Figma and Canva. I'm looking for a junior UI design role where I can keep learning and build real projects.

2. Why did you choose BSIT?

I chose BSIT because I wanted to combine design and technology. I like creating things that look good, and IT shows me how those things work for real users and real systems. I started with almost no IT knowledge, but that mix of creativity and technology is what keeps me interested.

3. What are your strongest IT skills?

My strongest skills right now are Excel data analysis and design tools. I completed a social media engagement analysis in Excel, and I explored Figma and Canva on my own, which led to my Plano app design. I'm still a beginner in all my skills, but these are the ones where I have the clearest evidence.

4. What is your weakest skill?

My weakest skill is coding, especially HTML and CSS. I'm still learning them, and I built my portfolio with AI assistance, so I'm practicing until I can write pages on my own.

5. Tell us about your major project.

My major project is Plano, a student-friendly study planner app that I first designed in Figma to help students organize their tasks, manage schedules, and track academic activities. The Figma design began with three screens: Login, Home, and Profile. The interactive web demo expands the design with a Tasks screen, task management, settings, and browser-based storage. I made it with AI assistance, and then reviewed the screens and the prototype myself. I chose a mobile app because I want to become a UI designer, and I wanted to practice clear layouts, consistent colors, and simple navigation.

6. What was your biggest technical problem?

The layout and code of my portfolio website. My first version didn't display properly because of small mistakes: a tag was missing its opening symbol, an empty tag stood where the body should have been, and my style rules were in the wrong place. My profile photo also didn't appear at first.

7. How did you solve it?

I read the code line by line, compared it with a correct version, and changed one thing at a time until it worked. It taught me patience and attention to detail, because one missing character can break a whole page.

8. How do you handle deadlines?

I start early and make a schedule, so I can finish step by step and still have time to review my work before the deadline.

9. How do you work with a team?

I've worked in groups several times during my BSIT program. I try to do my part on time, share my ideas, and communicate clearly with my teammates. I've learned that good communication matters as much as technical skill.

10. Why should an organization consider hiring you?

I'm honest about my level, and I back every skill with evidence. I'm a self-motivated learner: I taught myself Figma and Canva without anyone telling me to, and I've built a portfolio, a data project, and a Figma design. I also use AI responsibly by checking its work. I'll bring curiosity, a willingness to learn, and care for making things clear for users.

11. What technology are you currently learning?

I'm currently learning HTML and CSS and Figma prototyping. My goal is to build more complete Figma projects for my portfolio.

12. Where do you want to develop professionally?

I want to start as a Junior UI Designer, then grow into a UI/UX Designer who designs web and mobile experiences with confidence, combining creativity with my IT background.
